items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

Application.add_domain() compiled each * in a host mask to [^:]*. With two or more wildcards in a mask, matching a long Host header that does not match the mask took polynomial time on the event loop.

Impact

An attacker could stall a server that registers a domain mask with more than one wildcard by sending requests with a long Host header.

Workaround

Use at most one * in a domain mask.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/c6ac0e44c3c573ff9616f4a6a532992538b31e43

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

Set-Cookie parsing created additional cookies from unrecognised name=value attributes, and CookieJar had no limit on the number of cookies stored or sent. A server could make the client store a very large number of cookies and generate very large Cookie headers.

Impact

A malicious server could cause excessive memory and CPU use in a client, repeated on every redirect, and cause later requests to the same domain to build an excessively large Cookie header.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6963ee0befec1502b6bb7b4db6c72d044c08f4fa

Summary

Request.post() had no limit on the number of fields in a URL-encoded form body. Inserting a large number of repeated keys into a MultiDict took quadratic time on the event loop.

Impact

An attacker could block the event loop with a form POST within the default client_max_size to any handler that calls Request.post().

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

When reading a multipart part with Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, BodyPartReader.read_chunk() kept reading until the chunk length was a multiple of 4, with no byte limit. A part with a short Content-Length, or a long run of whitespace, could cause the entire remaining body to be read into memory within a single call before any size check, or spin on the event loop.

Impact

An attacker could bypass client_max_size to cause excessive memory use, or block the event loop, with a specially crafted multipart request to any handler that reads multipart data.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fdd

References

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

The max_msg_size check in the WebSocket reader added the declared frame length to the size of the partial message already buffered. In the C extension this addition is 64-bit arithmetic, so a declared length close to 2**63 overflowed and the check passed.

Impact

An attacker could bypass max_msg_size and cause unbounded memory use by streaming an oversized WebSocket message after a small non-final fragment.

Workaround

If unable to upgrade, the Python reader is unaffected and can be used with AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/8cfbe9abe5e11b84006a10f9bdf82bf607671dab

Affected versions

aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

While a request flagged as an upgrade (e.g. a WebSocket handshake) was being handled, all further data received on the connection was buffered with no size limit or flow control until the handler completed.

Impact

An attacker could cause unbounded memory use by streaming data behind an upgrade request to any handler that does not immediately accept or reject the upgrade.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/3d850ee9b92573c7e913821cbcb96005beb3f4df

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

When the pipelined request queue was full, the pure-Python parser stored the unparsed remainder internally and also returned it to the caller. After a handler declined an upgrade request, the buffered data was re-fed, so the buffer grew with each handled request and already-handled requests were dispatched to the application again.

Impact

If users are using the Python parser (AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS, or not a standard wheel installed), an attacker could cause excessive memory use and cause pipelined requests to be processed more than once.

Workaround

Switch to the default C parser.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/47babd8c23ca79e2bae6cc8dcb5752b61e369fc7

References

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

When decompressing a payload made up of many concatenated compressed members (gzip, deflate or zstd), each member was decoded by passing the entire remaining input to a new decompressor, resulting in quadratic CPU time. Empty members produce no output, so client_max_size and output backpressure did not limit the work.

Impact

An attacker could block the event loop of a server with a specially crafted compressed request body or WebSocket message. A malicious server could do the same to a client.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/d925a80539ffd227da1d93ab4a5bff123cc777db

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
aiohttp <= 3.14.3 3.14.4

Summary

The WebSocket reader continued parsing frames already received after the receive queue had paused the transport, and empty messages were not counted towards the queue size. With permessage-deflate, a single read of compressed frames could add many megabytes of decompressed messages to the queue.

Impact

An attacker could cause excessive memory use in a WebSocket server, or a malicious server against a client, by sending many small or compressed messages faster than the application consumes them.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/0ae507423f681161efa77d20052b4054397c7fb6

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
nltk < 3.10.4 No fix available

Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-gpwc-27cw-rh9r. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

NLTK from 3.6 before 3.10.4 contains an algorithmic complexity vulnerability in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize that allows remote attackers to exhaust CPU by supplying long all-vowel tokens. Attackers can submit a token such as a long run of vowels, causing the unguarded onset reversal loop to perform quadratic work and deny service to syllabification components.

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
nltk >= 3.9.4, <= 3.10.3 3.10.4

Summary

nltk.sem.chat80.sql_query() opens a SQLite database by handing the result of nltk.data.find(dbname) straight to sqlite3.connect() without the path-containment check that the NLTK data sandbox (nltk.pathsec) is meant to enforce. nltk.data.find() applies only lexical checks to the resource name and returns a FileSystemPathPointer whose path is normalized with os.path.abspath but never resolved for symlinks. As a result, an in-root symbolic link that points at a SQLite file outside every registered NLTK data root is followed by SQLite, and the caller receives query results from the out-of-sandbox database. An attacker who can place a file inside a directory the application trusts as an NLTK data root can read SQLite databases that the pathsec sandbox is supposed to keep out of reach.

Root Cause

The security invariant is that file access performed through NLTK data resolution must stay within the configured data roots; the sandbox enforces this in nltk.pathsec via validate_path and pathsec.open, which resolve the real path (Path(...).resolve()) and reject targets outside the allowed roots. sql_query() never reaches that enforcement point. It calls nltk.data.find(dbname), whose guards operate purely on the resource-name string, and FileSystemPathPointer.__init__ performs only os.path.abspath plus an existence check, which does not collapse symlinks. The pointer is then passed to sqlite3.connect(str(path)), so the containment decision that FileSystemPathPointer.open() would delegate to pathsec.open is bypassed entirely. The sibling functions in the same module that create or write databases (cities2table, val_dump, val_load) obtain their protection from a validation call in later development, but the read sink sql_query performs no equivalent check in any published release.

nltk/sem/chat80.py  -> sql_query(): path = nltk.data.find(dbname); sqlite3.connect(str(path))
nltk/data.py        -> find(): lexical name guards only; returns FileSystemPathPointer
nltk/data.py        -> FileSystemPathPointer.__init__(): os.path.abspath + os.path.exists (no symlink resolution)
nltk/data.py        -> FileSystemPathPointer.open() -> nltk.pathsec.open (the containment guard that sql_query never calls)

Impact

An attacker who can write into a directory the application registers as an NLTK data root (a shared or writable corpus directory, or a downloaded corpus) can plant a symbolic link at the expected resource location that points at a SQLite database elsewhere on the filesystem. When the application invokes sql_query() (directly or via sql_demo()) for that resource, SQLite follows the link and the query executes against the out-of-sandbox database, returning its rows to the caller. This escapes the pathsec confidentiality boundary. The read primitive is bounded to SQLite-format files that are readable by the process user: a non-SQLite target raises sqlite3.DatabaseError rather than leaking content. A caller-supplied write query would be redirected onto the out-of-sandbox target and SQLite may create sidecar files (-wal, -journal) next to it, which is a plausible integrity side effect rather than a demonstrated arbitrary-write primitive. Exploitation requires the same local write capability into a trusted data root as the related symlink-read sandbox-escape issues already recorded for this project.

Proof of Concept

Requires the published nltk 3.10.3 wheel and a writable directory registered as an NLTK data root. No network access is needed.

  1. Create a throwaway data root with the expected corpus subdirectory.
  2. Create a SQLite database outside that root and populate it.
  3. Plant an in-root symbolic link at corpora/city_database/city.db pointing at the outside database.
  4. Register the data root and call sql_query() for the in-root resource name.
import os, tempfile, sqlite3, nltk, nltk.data
from nltk.sem import chat80

work = tempfile.mkdtemp()
root = os.path.join(work, "nltk_data")
corp = os.path.join(root, "corpora", "city_database")
os.makedirs(corp)

secret = os.path.join(work, "outside", "secret.db")
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(secret))
con = sqlite3.connect(secret)
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t (x text)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES ('OUT-OF-SANDBOX-SECRET')")
con.commit(); con.close()

os.symlink(secret, os.path.join(corp, "city.db"))
nltk.data.path.insert(0, root)

ptr = nltk.data.find("corpora/city_database/city.db")
try:
    ptr.open().read()            # pathsec route: blocked
except Exception as e:
    print("open() blocked:", type(e).__name__)

cur = chat80.sql_query("corpora/city_database/city.db", "SELECT * FROM t")
print("sql_query rows:", cur.fetchall())   # sink route: follows the symlink

open() blocked: PermissionError
sql_query rows: [('OUT-OF-SANDBOX-SECRET',)]

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: The application exposes sql_query() (or sql_demo(), which calls it) and resolves the target database through nltk.data.find, using at least one directory the attacker can write to as a data root.
  2. Control: The attacker controls the on-disk object at the in-root resource path, replacing it with a symbolic link whose target is chosen freely. The resource-name argument stays a clean, in-root string.
  3. Path: nltk.data.find applies its lexical name guards (_UNSAFE_NO_PROTOCOL_RE, encoded and normalized-form checks), which inspect only the name string and pass, then returns a FileSystemPathPointer whose __init__ applies os.path.abspath and an existence check without resolving the symlink.
  4. Guard: The containment guard (FileSystemPathPointer.open() delegating to nltk.pathsec.open, which resolves the real path and rejects out-of-root targets) is never invoked, because sql_query() passes the raw pointer string to sqlite3.connect() instead of opening through the pointer.
  5. Primitive: sqlite3.connect(str(path)) opens the symlink target; the kernel follows the link out of every data root and the cursor executes the query against the outside database.
  6. Result: Rows from a SQLite database outside the sandbox are returned to the caller, escaping the pathsec confidentiality boundary for SQLite-format files readable by the process user.

Bypass Evidence

The relevant guard is the pathsec containment enforced by nltk.pathsec.open/validate_path, reached through FileSystemPathPointer.open(). On an identical pointer produced from the planted symlink, ptr.open() raises PermissionError with an "Unauthorized path" security violation, confirming the guard is active and correct for the sandbox route. sql_query() does not call .open() and does not call validate_path; it passes the unresolved pointer string directly to sqlite3.connect(), so the guard never runs on this path and the read succeeds. Attempts to invalidate the finding were made and failed: nltk.data.find was checked for a hidden containment or real-path resolution and has none (its guards are name-string only, and FileSystemPathPointer.__init__ uses abspath, not realpath); SQLite was confirmed to follow the link and read the outside file rather than opening the link node; and the possibility that an existing published fix already covers this sink was refuted by inspecting the published artifacts, where no containment check is present on sql_query. The behavior was reproduced against the exact published 3.10.3 wheel (verified by its published SHA-256 digest).

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: PyPI
  • Package: nltk
  • Confirmed affected range: >= 3.9.4, <= 3.10.3
  • Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, wheel SHA-256 ff9598a8e20518ee0d557745890cc4435b9578489e2dcbc69c4f81fa060caf7c)
  • Fix status: 3.10.4

The pathsec sandbox that this issue bypasses was introduced in 3.9.4; the immediately preceding release 3.9.3 does not ship nltk/pathsec.py and therefore does not present this sandbox-escape surface. Every published release from 3.9.4 through the current latest 3.10.3 ships nltk/pathsec.py with ENFORCE = True and ships sql_query() without any containment check, so all of them are affected. Each affected wheel was fetched from PyPI and inspected directly. No published release removes the sink or adds the guard, so no fixed version exists at the time of review.

Suggested Fix

Enforce the data-root containment invariant on the resolved database path before opening it. In sql_query(), validate the path through the same mechanism the sibling functions use (for example validate_path(str(path), context="chat80.sql_query")) or open the database through the pointer's sandboxed open path rather than passing the raw string to sqlite3.connect(). The remediation should resolve symbolic links (real-path resolution) and reject targets outside the registered data roots, and it should cover any other read sinks that connect to on-disk databases resolved through nltk.data.find. As an interim mitigation, applications should ensure that no attacker-writable directory is registered as an NLTK data root and should avoid calling sql_query/sql_demo on resources that live in shared or untrusted locations.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: IN PROGRESS (fix on an open pull request, not yet on develop).

PR: #3888 "Validate chat80.sql_query dbname for path containment (CWE-59/73)", open; head e0e890f51 at the time of this note. This is the same sink and vector as GHSA-xv54-447f-mj22 (now closed).

Fix commits: 9f5d2ea6d (sql_query calls validate_path before nltk.data.find, as cities2table, val_dump and val_load already do) and 47bd0476e (the file behind a sql_query resource name is resolved through the data roots and validated, and its store is pinned).

The advisory PoC (an in-root corpora/city_database/city.db symlink to an out-of-root SQLite file, resolved through find()) re-run on the PR head e0e890f51: refused with PermissionError (Security Violation [chat80.sql_query]: Unauthorized path, naming the symlink's resolved out-of-root target); the same resource name backed by a real in-root database still returns its rows on that head. On develop 2fa3f48fe the PoC returns the rows of the out-of-root database, so develop is VULNERABLE.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_xv54_447f_mj22.py on the PR (the sibling advisory GHSA-xv54-447f-mj22), FIXED on the PR head (absolute path, traversal and a symlink inside a scratch directory are all security-rejected). Those three cases are also rejected on develop by find() itself; the in-root symlink above is the case that only the PR closes.

Release: none.

References

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-xmfg-f9cm-w86q
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126302
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/nltk-3.9.4-before-3.10.4-symlink-sandbox-escape-via-chat80-sql-query
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmfg-f9cm-w86q

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
nltk <= 3.10.3 3.10.4

Summary

Path traversal in NLTK's save_maxent_params() and load_maxent_params() allows arbitrary file write and arbitrary file read outside the directories permitted by NLTK's pathsec security mechanism.

This vulnerability was previously reported through Huntr, accepted by the NLTK project, and assigned CVE-2026-15367. A $750 bounty was paid through Huntr (i didnt get the fix bounty). Huntr subsequently shut down its OSS vulnerability program, so I am submitting this report through GitHub to continue the existing disclosure process and preserve the original CVE assignment and researcher credit.

Details

The affected functions are:

  • nltk.classify.maxent.load_maxent_params()
  • nltk.classify.maxent.save_maxent_params()

Both functions construct filesystem paths from the caller-controlled tab_dir argument and access them using Python's built-in open() without passing the paths through NLTK's pathsec validation.

For example, load_maxent_params() constructs and opens:

  • /weights.txt
  • /mapping.tab
  • /labels.txt
  • /alwayson.tab

Similarly, save_maxent_params() creates/writes files under the supplied tab_dir.

This bypasses the security boundary provided by nltk.pathsec. NLTK documents pathsec as the mechanism for restricting filesystem access to permitted roots, with strict enforcement intended to prevent unauthorized filesystem access.

The relevant implementation is in:

nltk/classify/maxent.py

The affected functions can be found in the model parameter loading/saving section of that file.

This issue was previously disclosed through Huntr and accepted before the Huntr OSS program was shut down. The original Huntr report was assigned CVE-2026-15367 and received a $750 bounty.

I am therefore submitting this GitHub Security Advisory primarily as a continuation/transfer of the existing disclosure rather than as a new vulnerability report.

PoC

The issue can be reproduced by enabling NLTK's path security enforcement and supplying a tab_dir outside the permitted root.

For example, with a controlled test environment:

import os
import tempfile
import nltk.pathsec as pathsec
from nltk.classify.maxent import load_maxent_params, save_maxent_params

pathsec.ENFORCE = True

allowed_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
outside_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()

# The same outside-root path is rejected when accessed through pathsec.
try:
    with pathsec.open(os.path.join(outside_dir, "test.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write("test")
except Exception as e:
    print("pathsec.open rejected outside-root access:", type(e).__name__)

# The vulnerable model-parameter APIs directly use open()
# on paths derived from tab_dir.
#
# Supplying outside_dir as tab_dir causes the functions to access
# files under outside_dir rather than enforcing the pathsec boundary.

For save_maxent_params(), the attacker-controlled tab_dir determines where the model parameter files are written.

For load_maxent_params(), the attacker-controlled tab_dir determines which files are read.

The important security property being bypassed is that pathsec.ENFORCE = True does not protect these file operations because the affected functions call the built-in open() directly rather than the pathsec-aware file-opening mechanism.

Impact

This is a path traversal / filesystem sandbox bypass resulting in arbitrary local file read and arbitrary local file write.

Applications that use NLTK's pathsec mechanism as a filesystem security boundary may incorrectly assume that model parameter loading and saving are restricted to approved directories.

An attacker who can influence the tab_dir argument may therefore:

  • read files outside the permitted NLTK data directories through load_maxent_params();
  • create or overwrite files outside the permitted directories through save_maxent_params();
  • bypass the filesystem containment provided by nltk.pathsec.

The practical impact depends on how an application exposes these APIs and what filesystem permissions the NLTK process has.

Existing CVE / Disclosure History

CVE: CVE-2026-15367

This vulnerability was previously reported and accepted through Huntr before the Huntr OSS vulnerability program was shut down. The report received a $750 bounty and a CVE was reserved.

I am submitting this report because the original Huntr disclosure workflow is no longer available and the CVE has not yet been published.

Please associate this report with CVE-2026-15367 rather than assigning a new CVE, unless the NLTK maintainers determine that the existing CVE does not correspond to this issue.

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop. The load side is in every release since 3.9.4 (including v3.10.3); the save side is on develop and unreleased.

Fix commits: f2556f9e1 (load_maxent_params reads through open_datafile on a PathPointer whose open is pathsec.open; contained in tag 3.9.4 and every later tag) and 2a92b7182 (save_maxent_params validates tab_dir and writes every parameter file through pathsec.open), PR #3759 "Harden maxent / named-entity model-artifact saves against shared-tmp planting", merged 2026-08-18, merge commit a167e94bc on develop.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_59f9_gqg8_mqpj.py, added on the open PR #3753 (head da55cab0e at the time of this note; measured on its earlier head 238f81500) together with commit 15f84f036 (load_maxent_params accepts a plain str or Path through FileSystemPathPointer). Verdict on 238f81500: FIXED (save and load outside every data root refused by pathsec). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe reports the save refused and a PathPointer load refused, while a str or Path tab_dir raises AttributeError before any file is opened (the probe counts that crash as not fixed; no file is read or written).

References

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
nltk <= 3.10.3 3.10.4

Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

Root Cause

matchBrackets consumes a bracket body one character at a time with inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]. The rest = rest[1:] tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). augParseCategory drives a while rest != "": operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (rest = app[3]) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.

Affected functions:
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)
Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.

Impact

An attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.

Proof of Concept

Environment: nltk 3.10.3, regex 2026.9.10, CPython. Run the parser on the shipped public API.

import nltk.ccg.lexicon as L

# Vector A: flat bracket body -> matchBrackets tail re-slice is O(n^2)
n = 400000
lex_a = ":- S\nw => (" + "a" * n + ")\n"

# Vector B: long operator chain -> augParseCategory tail re-copy is O(n^2)
m = 32000
lex_b = ":- a\nw => " + "a" + "/a" * m + "\n"

import time
for name, s in (("A", lex_a), ("B", lex_b)):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        L.fromstring(s)
    except Exception:
        pass  # downstream parse error is irrelevant; the CPU is already burned
    print(name, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")

Negative control (":- a\nw => (a/a)"):   ~0.00007 s
Vector A (matchBrackets, flat body):     n=50k 0.078s | 100k 0.260s | 200k 1.046s | 400k 2.083s   (~4x per doubling => O(n^2))
Vector B (augParseCategory, operators):  m=4k 0.078s | 8k 0.215s | 16k 0.485s | 32k 1.329s        (super-linear)

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: An application calls the public nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str) (also reachable as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring) on lexicon text the attacker can influence.
  2. Control: The attacker fully controls the body width (a run of characters inside one bracket) and the operator-chain length; neither is capped by fromstring.
  3. Path: fromstring splits input into lines and routes each category through nextCategory, which dispatches to matchBrackets (Vector A) or into the augParseCategory operator loop (Vector B).
  4. Guard: The only relevant guard is the MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500 recursion-depth check. On flat input the recursion depth is zero, so if _depth > max_depth is never reached; the width loops run unbounded.
  5. Primitive: The tail re-slice rest = rest[1:] and tail re-copy rest = app[3] execute a quadratic number of string copies.
  6. Result: Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a few-megabyte lexicon costs tens of seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the parsing thread.

Bypass Evidence

The one protection present on this path is the recursion-depth guard MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500 (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:22), checked at lexicon.py:153 and lexicon.py:228. It defends only against nesting depth and raises a bounded ValueError for deeply nested categories. The quadratic payloads here are flat: a single bracket body or a single operator run has nesting depth zero to one, so the depth check provably never fires while the width loops consume quadratic time. This was confirmed by running the shipped parser: the payloads complete without a ValueError or a regex TimeoutError while consuming quadratic CPU (Vector A shows a clean 4x cost per input doubling). A repository search finds no line-length or category-width cap anywhere on the fromstring path; the regex source-length limit bounds regex patterns, not lexicon text. The strongest disproof attempt (that CPython in-place string concatenation makes Vector A linear) fails because rest = rest[1:] is an unconditional copy of the remaining input that the concatenation fast path cannot elide, and the measured 4x-per-doubling ratio confirms the quadratic empirically.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)
  • Package: nltk
  • Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3
  • Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)
  • Fix status: 3.10.4

The width-slicing loops ship in every release carrying the CCG lexicon parser and are present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior long predates the recent regular-expression and recursion-depth hardening.

Suggested Fix

Scan the bracket body and the operator chain with an index cursor into the original string (or a collections.deque) instead of repeatedly re-slicing or re-copying the tail, so each character is handled in constant amortized time. As defense in depth, impose an explicit bound on lexicon line length and category width at the fromstring chokepoint and raise a bounded error when it is exceeded, mirroring the existing depth guard. No configuration-only mitigation fully removes the exposure for a service that must parse untrusted lexicons; until a fix ships, callers should cap the size of accepted lexicon input and parse it under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Fix status

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py: matchBrackets, nextCategory and augParseCategory thread a cursor instead of re-slicing the tail; the trailing capture group is dropped; MAX_PARSE_LEN=100000 caps the input).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_89p3_fcch_88ph.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (scaling 4.4x over a 4x input; an over-cap chain is rejected by MAX_PARSE_LEN). The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe: vector A (bracket body, 100k vs 400k) 15.8x and vector B (operator chain, 8k vs 32k) 11.3x over a 4x input, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

References

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-89p3-fcch-88ph
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126299
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/3944
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/0bb5b947bd235b950cf2f90e893a498e16da0fe3
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/cf12a5e6a
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/releases/tag/v3.10.4
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/nltk-before-3.10.4-quadratic-time-denial-of-service-via-ccg-lexicon-fromstring
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-89p3-fcch-88ph

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
nltk <= 3.10.3 3.10.4

Summary

Tree.chomsky_normal_form() binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with list.pop(0), which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode] inside a loop over the N children of a node. list.pop(0) is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses nodeCopy.pop() (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public Tree.fromstring parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.

Affected function:
- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)
Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).

Impact

An attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not wrap this pure-Python list loop.

Proof of Concept

Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Drive the public transform on a wide flat tree.

import time
from nltk.tree import Tree

for N in (80000, 160000, 320000):
    s = "(S " + "(A a)" * N + ")"
    t = Tree.fromstring(s)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    t.chomsky_normal_form()          # default factor="right"
    print("right", N, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3), "s")

right (default):  N=80000 1.972s | N=160000 5.004s (2.54x) | N=320000 14.518s (2.90x)   -> super-linear
left  (control):  N=80000 1.399s | N=160000 2.731s (1.95x) | N=320000  5.379s (1.97x)   -> linear

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: An application parses an attacker-influenced treebank string with the public Tree.fromstring and normalizes it with Tree.chomsky_normal_form().
  2. Control: The attacker controls the number of children of a node (a wide flat tree such as (S (A a)(A a)...(A a))); no child-count cap exists in fromstring or the transform.
  3. Path: Tree.chomsky_normal_form delegates to nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form with the default factor="right".
  4. Guard: None. There is no width bound on the loop, and the regex match timeout does not wrap this pure-Python list operation.
  5. Primitive: curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode] performs an O(N) front shift on each of N iterations.
  6. Result: O(N^2) single-core CPU exhaustion; roughly 1.5 MB of input costs about 14 seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the processing thread.

Bypass Evidence

There is no guard to bypass on this path: neither Tree.fromstring nor chomsky_normal_form caps the child count, and the regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps only regex matching, not this list loop. The finding was confirmed by fresh timing that isolates the cause: the right-factor default and the left-factor branch build the identical bounded head strings and copy the node once, so the only differing term is pop(0) versus pop(). The measured right-versus-left divergence grows with N (right rises toward a 4x per-doubling ratio while left holds near 2x), which proves a quadratic component beyond the shared linear costs. A relevant corroboration is that the inverse transform un_chomsky_normal_form was already rewritten to a single linear pass to remove exactly this quadratic class (see the comment at nltk/tree/transforms.py:195-201), while the forward default path retained the pop(0) idiom. The strongest disproof attempt (that the head-string join dominates and is linear) fails because that join is bounded and present in both branches and therefore cannot explain the branch-dependent quadratic growth.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)
  • Package: nltk
  • Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3
  • Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)
  • Fix status: 3.10.4

The right-factor pop(0) idiom ships in every release carrying this transform and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open.

Suggested Fix

Rewrite the right-factor binarization to avoid removing from the front of a list: iterate the children with an index cursor or a collections.deque so each step is constant time, mirroring the linear rebuild already applied to un_chomsky_normal_form. As defense in depth, bound the child count accepted for normalization and raise a clear error past a configurable maximum. No configuration-only mitigation removes the exposure for a service that normalizes untrusted trees; until a fix ships, callers should cap accepted tree width and run the transform under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3909 "Fix quadratic DoS in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization (GHSA-r53h-rw34-8h97)", merged 2026-09-23, merge commit 2f53e20ce on develop.

Fix commits: 457ebe349 (linear front consume in chomsky_normal_form) and 677857dca (refuse a binarisation that would nest a tree beyond MAX_TREE_DEPTH). Follow-up #3917 (merge 9ba132e43, commit f0686dea6) walks Tree equality and conversion with an explicit stack so the deep-tree tests pass on Python 3.10 and 3.11.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_r53h_rw34_8h97.py; verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (chomsky_normal_form scales 5.1x over a 4x input).

References

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-r53h-rw34-8h97
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126298
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/3909
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/457ebe349f8dd8080224f76a64aff806dd437057
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/677857dcafd84e4591865d976b562a27dfde566e
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/releases/tag/v3.10.4

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
nltk <= 3.10.3 3.10.4

Summary

ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances() builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

Root Cause

_get_srl_instances iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner break that stops only when a span tagged V or C-V containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the for ... else: continue construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.

Affected function:
- nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:394-424; nested rescan at lines 405-419)
Public entry point: nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:158-169).

Impact

An attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with srl_instances() causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost is super-linear in attacker-chosen predicate and column counts, a roughly 1 MB crafted corpus pins a core for tens of seconds and a few megabytes reaches minutes. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not cover this pure-Python nested loop over the parsed grid. Exploitation requires the application to use the SRL-specific API on untrusted CoNLL data with words, pos, tree, and srl columns; a deployment that never calls srl_instances() is unaffected.

Proof of Concept

Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Stage a crafted CoNLL corpus under an authorized data root and iterate srl_instances().
Corpus construction: one blank-line-delimited block with P predicate rows and P SRL span columns, the sole "V" head span in the last column.

import time, os, tempfile
from nltk.corpus.reader.conll import ConllCorpusReader

def build_block(n):
    # n predicates, n SRL columns; the single V head placed in the last column
    # (columns: words pos tree srl...): emit n predicate rows and n SRL span
    # columns, with the single "V" head span placed in the final column.
    ...

for n in (40, 80, 160, 320):
    root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(root, "c.conll"), "w").write(build_block(n))
    r = ConllCorpusReader(root, ["c.conll"], ("words", "pos", "tree", "srl"))
    t = time.perf_counter()
    list(r.srl_instances())
    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")

Negative control (single predicate): n=40 -> 1.88 ms ; n=320 -> 4.45 ms      (flat)
Attack (P=R=n):  n=40 -> 0.022s (10 KB) | n=80 -> 0.148s (39 KB) | n=160 -> 1.164s (156 KB) | n=320 -> 10.002s (619 KB)

The attack timing rises about 8x per doubling of n while the file grows only about 4x, confirming super-linear cost driven by attacker-chosen predicate and column count; the single-predicate control stays in the millisecond range.

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: An application loads an attacker-supplied CoNLL corpus (columns include srl) and iterates it with the public ConllCorpusReader(...).srl_instances().
  2. Control: The attacker controls the predicate count P, the span-column count, and the placement of the single head span; the block is read whole with no size cap.
  3. Path: srl_instances() calls _get_srl_instances, which pairs each predicate against the span columns via a doubly-nested scan.
  4. Guard: The inner break on the first matching V or C-V head is defeated by placing the sole head span in the last column, so every earlier column is scanned in full. The path-containment sandbox bounds where files load, not how much work a block costs.
  5. Primitive: The nested rescan performs O(P^2 * R) span comparisons with no work cap or timeout.
  6. Result: Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a roughly 1 MB corpus costs tens of seconds and scales super-linearly, blocking the processing thread.

Bypass Evidence

The only short-circuit on this path is the inner break that fires when a predicate's V or C-V head span is found. It is defeated by construction: placing the sole head span in the last span column means no earlier column matches, so the for ... else: continue traverses every span of every earlier column for every predicate. This was confirmed in source (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:405-419) and reproduced end-to-end through the real public srl_instances() API, where the attack timing scales super-linearly while a single-predicate control stays flat. The path-containment sandbox is a file-location control and imposes no bound on parse cost, and the regular-expression timeout does not wrap this loop. The strongest disproof attempts (that Python range membership is O(1) so the loop is linear, and that the break fires early) both fail: the O(1) membership test is evaluated once per span, and the number of spans traversed is exactly what the last-column head placement maximizes.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)
  • Package: nltk
  • Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3
  • Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)
  • Fix status: 3.10.4

The nested rescan ships in every release carrying this reader and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior predates the recent regular-expression hardening.

Suggested Fix

Replace the per-predicate linear search over all span columns with a single pass that indexes head spans by word position (for example, build a map from word index to the owning span column once, then look up each predicate in constant time), reducing the total cost to about O(P * R). As defense in depth, bound the predicate and span counts accepted from a single block and process untrusted corpora under a CPU or time budget. No configuration-only mitigation removes the exposure for a service that must read untrusted CoNLL SRL data; until a fix ships, callers should cap accepted corpus size and isolate the parsing worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a "Patch seven algorithmic-DoS and path/exec GHSA classes across all affected modules" (ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances builds a one-pass wordnum to spanlist index instead of rescanning per predicate).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_v8f3_6phw_6mh9.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (srl_instances scaled 3.9x over 4x predicates). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe: VULNERABLE (45.8x over 4x predicates).

Original Description

NLTK before 3.10.4 contains a quadratic-time denial of service vulnerability in ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances that allows remote attackers to exhaust CPU through nested span rescans. Attackers can supply a crafted CoNLL SRL corpus with many predicates and span columns, placing the head span last, to pin a core for minutes.
